errors.english: refers to the two aspects of the object and the cognition related to the object
errors.why: Substance is what can accomplish, without depending on anything else, the two kinds of purpose (of the object and of the related cognition); the two purposes are what it accomplishes, not what 'substance' refers to.

errors.english: Those things established as the basis for the phenomena and subject are the second category.
errors.why: The properties and property-bearers that take the quality as their basis are the second kind; the English reverses which is the basis.

note: A sound rendering of the substance/quality section; two clauses are construed wrongly.

errors.english: If this were to change, these two would not be the same.
errors.why: This finishes the previous sentence ('so too would this come about'), and then asserts that the two cases are not alike; nothing 'changes', and the dissimilarity is asserted, not conditional.

errors.english: However, as for what is explained here regarding diversity: "diverse is not present in each, because they are not diverse"
errors.why: The Tibetan says variegatedness does not inhere in the composite whole where conjunction exists, and the root line explaining this is 'because each [part] is not variegated'; the English garbles the claim and the quoted line.

errors.english: Well then, how is fire perceived as fire?
errors.why: This opens the opponent's analogy ('Suppose: just as, when fire has been grasped as fire...'), not a question.

note: The argument against the variegated cognition can be followed, but the opening and the opponent's analogy are construed wrongly.

errors.english: they become like a living presence
errors.why: skyes here is 'a gift': when he meets noble people, his words become like a gift.
mi bshes pa means unacquainted people (strangers, as the gloss itself explains), not hostile ones.

note: A faithful rendering of the word-by-word commentary, with two lexical slips.

errors.english: if the wisdom of the (Tathagata) Thus Gone One, which is non-conceptual toward all objects, does not fully understand the three natures, it will not be realized
errors.why: The Tathāgata's non-conceptual wisdom is what is not realized if one does not fully understand the three natures; it is not the wisdom that fails to understand them.

fix.find: if the wisdom of the (Tathagata) Thus Gone One, which is non-conceptual toward all objects, does not fully understand the three natures, it will not be realized
fix.replace: the wisdom of the (Tathagata) Thus Gone One, which is non-conceptual toward all objects, is not realized if one does not fully understand the three natures

errors.english: Because they are superimpositions of what does exist
errors.why: They are 'imagined' because they superimpose what does not exist.

fix.replace: superimpositions of what does not exist

note: The Yogācāra vocabulary is good, but two clauses, one of them central to the definition of the imagined nature, say the wrong thing.

errors.english: the body of those with blind minds is thinned day by day by limbs that fail to see faults
errors.why: It is the body, which lacks the faculty of seeing faults, that grows thinner day by day; the limbs are not the agent of the thinning.

errors.english: one should view them with the perception of a sister. The wise should completely turn away from such things.
errors.why: The four-line summary verse has one subject: the wise man, regarding her as a sister, should turn away from her. The English turns it into prose and splits it into two injunctions.

errors.english: those who commit non-virtuous actions with their noisy senses will suffer.
errors.why: This phrase is part of a description of hell-torments that continues onto the next side; 'noisy senses' is not in the Tibetan, and the sentence is closed off with an invented conclusion.

note: The prose rendering of the kāvya verses gives the gist, but several clauses are misconstrued.

errors.english: this specifically indicates that it does not refer to the non-subsequent words
errors.why: The text is specified here as applying 'to the statement that has no subsequent one' (the final one); the English negates it.

note: A good Vinaya rendering with correct karmavācanā terminology (jñapti, sīmā, Upāli); one clause is inverted.
A faithful translation; the patriarchal lineage and the Vaibhāṣika objection are rendered correctly.

errors.english: Regardless of which term one considers, the conclusion is drawn from that very cause
errors.why: This is a grammatical gloss: in correlation with the relative word 'gang' (yat), 'from that cause' (tasmāt) is to be supplied.
gom pa is habituation (abhyāsa), not vāsanā (bag chags).
With 'gog pa' on the next side, 'It is not so' refutes the doubt; it does not raise one.

note: The humoral argument can be followed, but the grammatical glosses are misread and one key term is mislabelled.

span_why: The opening sentences are not translated: tadutpatti is uncertain because it occurs only occasionally, so the capacity to indicate is uncertain, and the question 'from what [does it follow]?' answered by 'gal te'.

errors.english: He says: "It is not a negation."
errors.why: This means the refutation is the root phrase 'it is not'; it does not say 'it is not a negation'.

note: Accurate pramāṇa terminology (tādātmya, tadutpatti, saṃyoga) apart from one misread gloss, but the side's opening is missing.

errors.english: If it is free from dependence and is known, will it not fail to arise even slightly?
errors.why: The objection is that if cognition lacked a support (object), it would not arise at all.

errors.english: because it is secluded and free from other things
errors.why: Existence does not appear [by itself] because it lacks isolation from other things; the English says it is isolated.

note: The dream/waking argument is broadly rendered, but the passage on cognizing absence is muddled in places.
